texts.orig: To build this agent, you’d typically start by selecting an LLM (e.g. GPT-4o, Claude, or Gemini) and then design prompts (specific instructions) that guide the LLM to interpret user requests and respond appropriately. Your first impulse might be to feed user questions into the LLM directly to get out responses one by one, as with a simple chatbot, before adding capabilities to turn it into a true “agent.” When you extend your LLM-plus-prompt by giving it access to external tools—like flight APIs, hotel databases, or mapping services—you allow it to execute tasks, retrieve information, and respond dynamically to user requests. At that point, your simple LLM-plus-prompt evolves into an AI agent, capable of handling complex, multi-step interactions with your users. For internal testing, you might experiment with common scenarios and manually verify that the outputs make sense.

texts.orig: What exactly are evals?
texts.text: What exactly are evals?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Evals are how you measure the quality and effectiveness of your AI system. They act like regression tests or benchmarks, clearly defining what “good” actually looks like for your AI product beyond the kind of simple latency or pass/fail checks you’d usually use for software.
texts.text: Evals are how you measure the quality and effectiveness of your AI system. They act like regression tests or benchmarks, clearly defining what “good” actually looks like for your AI product beyond the kind of simple latency or pass/fail checks you’d usually use for software.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Evaluating AI systems is less like traditional software testing and more like giving someone a driving test:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Awareness:

texts.label: text

texts.label: text

texts.text: Decision-making:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Does it reliably make the correct choices, even in unpredictable situations?
texts.text: Does it reliably make the correct choices, even in unpredictable situations?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Safety:
texts.text: Safety:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Can it consistently follow directions and arrive safely at the intended destination, without going off the rails?
texts.text: Can it consistently follow directions and arrive safely at the intended destination, without going off the rails?

texts.label: text

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Evals are analogous to unit testing in some ways, with important differences. Traditional software unit testing is like checking if a train stays on its tracks: straightforward, deterministic, clear pass/fail scenarios. Evals for LLM-based systems, on the other hand, can feel more like driving a car through a busy city. The environment is variable, and the system is non-deterministic. Unlike in traditional software testing, when you give the same prompt to an LLM multiple times, you might see slightly different responses—just like how drivers can behave differently in city traffic. With evals, you’re often dealing with more qualitative or open-ended metrics—like the relevance or coherence of the output—that might not fit neatly into a strict pass/fail testing model.

LLM-based evals allow you to generate classification labels in an automated way that resembles human-labeled data—without needing to have users or subject-matter experts label all of your data.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Pro:
texts.text: Pro:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Highly scalable (it’s like a human labeling your data but much cheaper) and uses natural language, so PMs can write prompts directly. You can get the LLM to generate explanations for its judgments, making them more reliable and explainable for debugging. While individual judgments may be subjective, they become empirically useful over large datasets—if a human can grade something, so can an LLM. Production systems often use techniques like confidence scores or panels of LLM judges to increase reliability.

texts.text: Common mistakes I’ve seen teams make when adopting evals:

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Making evals too complex too quickly can create “noisy” signals (and cause the team to lose trust in the approach). Focus on specific outputs rather than complex evaluations—you can always add sophistication later.
texts.text: Making evals too complex too quickly can create “noisy” signals (and cause the team to lose trust in the approach). Focus on specific outputs rather than complex evaluations—you can always add sophistication later.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Not testing for edge cases. Provide one or two specific examples of “good” and “bad” evals as part of your prompt—few-shot prompting—for increased eval performance. This helps ground the judge-LLM in what is considered good or bad.
texts.text: Not testing for edge cases. Provide one or two specific examples of “good” and “bad” evals as part of your prompt—few-shot prompting—for increased eval performance. This helps ground the judge-LLM in what is considered good or bad.

texts.label: list_item
texts.orig: Forgetting to validate eval results against real user feedback. Remember that you’re not just testing code, you’re validating if your AI can truly solve user problems.
